title: How the Mona Lisa Heist Turned a Painting Into a Superstar—and a New Lloyd Webber Musical
summary: Before 1911, the Mona Lisa was just another old painting in the Louvre. Sure, art scholars admired it, but the general public barely noticed. Then, on August 21, an Italian housepainter named Vincenzo Peruggia walked out of the museum with the 30-inch portrait hidden under his smock, and everything changed. The theft was almost comically simple. Peruggia had helped install the protective glass case around the painting, so he knew precisely how to remove it. He waited until the museum was closed, blended in with other workers, lifted the Mona Lisa off the wall, and carried it to a stairwell. There, he separated it from its heavy frame and slipped away. It took 28 hours for anyone to realize the painting was missing—and only because an artist arrived to sketch it and found an empty wall. The ensuing investigation was chaotic. Police questioned everyone from museum staff to Pablo Picasso. They even interviewed Peruggia at his apartment, where the masterpiece sat in a trunk, but he didn't arouse suspicion. For two years, the Mona Lisa was nowhere to be found. Meanwhile, thousands of curious visitors, including Franz Kafka, flocked to the Louvre just to stare at the blank space. The painting's absence made it a sensation. In 1913, Peruggia contacted an art dealer in Florence, demanding a ransom. He claimed he wanted to return the painting to Italy, believing Napoleon had stolen it. (He hadn't; Leonardo da Vinci himself had brought it to France.) Peruggia was arrested, but many Italians hailed him as a patriot. He served a short sentence and the Mona Lisa returned to Paris, now the most famous artwork on Earth. Now, Andrew Lloyd Webber—the composer behind The Phantom of the Opera and Cats—is turning this stranger-than-fiction tale into a musical. He mentioned it almost offhandedly while promoting another show, calling it "a true story about how the Mona Lisa disappeared... and ended up in Italy." With Lloyd Webber's flair for spectacle, the heist that made the Mona Lisa a superstar might just become a theatrical one.
why_it_matters: The heist shows how value and fame sometimes come from absence and storytelling—an artwork that was once overlooked became an icon because it went missing, and now that story is being retold for a new generation through musical theater.

background_read: The Louvre in Paris is the largest art museum in the world, home to thousands of works including the Mona Lisa.

Leonardo da Vinci, the Italian Renaissance genius, painted the portrait around 1503-1506 and brought it with him to France when King Francis I invited him—so it wasn't stolen by Napoleon, contrary to the thief's belief.
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who conquered much of Europe but he did not steal the painting; that myth persisted for over a century.
Andrew Lloyd Webber, the composer behind Cats and The Phantom of the Opera, often turns historical or literary stories into musicals, blending spectacle with emotion.

perspectives.description: The theft accidentally turned the Mona Lisa into a global treasure, and the odd story now inspires art in another form. Audiences may gain interest in art history and museum security because of this legend.
Peruggia was ultimately a criminal who stole cultural heritage for a misguided cause; glorifying the theft in a musical might romanticize lawlessness and oversimplify historical wrongs.

The event demonstrates the social construction of value—crowds only cared because of absence. It also reveals how powerful myths (like Napoleon stealing the painting) can drive real-world actions long after they're debunked.

A musical could spark renewed debate about art repatriation and inspire museums to rethink how they market their collections. The show might also set a template for turning other famous thefts into entertainment.
